Because the mechanism fixes the set of schools I could possibly be matched with (my "Obtainable Schools") regardless of how I rank them, my ranking cannot change which schools are obtainable. It only chooses which school I receive among that fixed set — specifically, the highest-ranked school from that set.

Given that, the dominant strategy is to rank the schools in my true preference order so that, once the obtainable set is realized, I get the most-preferred school within it. I prefer w > y > z > x.

Additional checks: many other applicants favor y > x > w > z, but that only affects which schools are in my obtainable set (which the problem states is fixed given others' rankings) — it does not change that I should list my true ordering. I also have top priority (priority 1) at w and y, so if either is in my obtainable set I will receive the higher-ranked of those two; since I prefer w to y, I put w first. Between z and x I prefer z, so z comes before x.
reasoning.Student B:
Key property: the mechanism fixes a set of schools you could possibly be matched with (your Obtainable Schools) based on others' rankings and schools' priorities. Your submitted ranking cannot change which schools are in that set; it only determines which school you get among those obtainable (you receive your highest-ranked school in that set).

Given that, the best strategy is to list schools in true preference order, because you cannot make an unattainable school become obtainable by ranking it higher, nor make an obtainable school unobtainable by ranking it lower. You only influence which one of the obtainable schools you end up with — so you should put your true favorite among them first.

Notes on context: many applicants favor y > x > w > z, so y is likely to be heavily demanded and may be unattainable for you (your priority at y is 2). You have top priority (1) at x and z, and lower priority (2) at w and y. Even if x or z are more likely obtainable for you, you still prefer y and w over x, so you should rank according to your true preferences.

Therefore submit the truthful preference ordering: y > w > z > x.

It only chooses, from that fixed set, the highest-ranked school on my submitted list.

Given that, the dominant/obvious strategy is to rank schools in true preference order. Doing so ensures that, whatever the (fixed) obtainable set turns out to be, I will receive the most-preferred school within that set. Trying to “game” the order (e.g., promoting a less-preferred school to try to influence assignment) cannot expand the obtainable set and therefore cannot improve my outcome.

Note: my priorities (w:3, x:3, y:4, z:4) and the fact most applicants favor y > x > w > z suggest y (and possibly x) may be oversubscribed relative to my priority, but since my ranking cannot change which schools are obtainable, I should still submit my true preference ordering so I get the best available school from the fixed obtainable set.
